title: Cryptographic Misuse and Verification
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Cryptographic Misuse and Verification.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Cryptographic Misuse and Verification and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Cryptographic Misuse and Verification, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 16: Cryptography, Secrets, and Data Protection. It builds practical understanding of Cryptographic Misuse and Verification with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Cryptographic Misuse and Verification makes secure behavior repeatable across implementation, dependencies, configuration, and release. Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Cryptographic Misuse and Verification can be understood through this sequence: Classify protected data → Use vetted crypto → Scope and rotate keys → Verify exposure paths. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 123.1 Weak or obsolete algorithms; 123.2 Improper certificate validation; 123.3 Hardcoded or reused keys; 123.4 Insecure random-number generation; 123.5 Cryptographic implementation review; 123.6 Testing encryption and integrity controls. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local/owned application or explicitly authorized test target. Record only sanitized synthetic evidence; use human review for behavior that a static snippet cannot prove.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Cryptographic Misuse and Verification”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Cryptographic Misuse and Verification in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Cryptographic Misuse and Verification is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
